alternatives.explanation: Truncated exposure (definition and timing). Lapse means 'no order in year t+1', so most lapsers actually stop part-way through year t. Their year-t lines are cut short and fall in whichever months they were still active. Comparing annual short share and annual return counts across groups that are exposed for different lengths of time can produce effects in either direction. F8's sub-1 ratios (6-10% short share at 0.702, returns at 0.904 and 0.849) may be produced by this rather than mean anything.
alternatives.test: (a) Re-ran the annual design with short lines measured against what each customer's own branch-month mix would predict (observed short / expected short), also stratified by line volume. (b) Replaced the annual design with a fixed window: for each customer-quarter 2017Q1-2024Q4, exposure is that quarter's month-adjusted short ratio and the outcome is no order in the next 4 quarters, stratified by quarter x branch x trade x order band x line band (strata of 5 or more).
alternatives.result: (a) The annual design now shows a dose-response going the other way. Customers with 2x+ their expected short rate lapsed at 1.302 times expected (223 vs 171.3, n=2,007, order band 3+, q349). Among customers with 30+ lines it was 1.522 (85 vs 55.9, n=799), against 0.835 at under 1x (q351). Zero-short customers were also elevated (1.467, n=1,160), a U-shape that fits truncation rather than an effect. (b) In the fixed-window design the gradient disappears: 0.98 for no shorts (n=45,383), 1.059 under 1x, 1.078 at 1-2x, 1.042 at 2-4x and 1.028 at 4x+ (122 vs 118.7, n=3,269) (q354). The null survives, but on the fixed-window evidence. The annual-design ratios F8 cites are unreliable in both directions.

alternatives.explanation: Returns may look protective only because of the same exposure artefact, or the right test may be service-type returns specifically. erp_returns does carry a reason_code, despite the primer.
alternatives.test: Ran the same fixed quarterly window, splitting quarters by whether they had a 'damaged' or 'wrong item' return, only other returns, or none.
alternatives.result: No protective effect and no harmful one either. Damaged or wrong-item returns: 1.111 (36 vs 32.4, n=1,665). Other returns only: 1.106 (50 vs 45.2, n=2,296). No return: 0.996 (n=69,930) (q361). The reason codes are spread almost evenly across five values (1,247-1,328 each, q346), so they may not record real causes. That is a data-quality concern. The 'returns reduce lapse' reading should be dropped: returns are simply not associated with lapse.

alternatives.explanation: The 2016 excess might be a real stock-out effect rather than only a timing artefact.
alternatives.test: (a) Ran the fixed quarterly window restricted to 2016 quarters, with month-adjusted short ratio. (b) Took January cohorts each year: share of January lines short vs no order in the following 12 months, 2016 compared with other years.
alternatives.result: (a) There is a modest gradient in 2016: 0.895 under 1x, 1.088 at 1-2x and 1.202 at 2x+ (64 vs 53.3, n=1,140) (q356), far below the 2.061 in q292. (b) Only 57 of 2,573 January-2016 customers stopped for 12 months. The ratio was not monotone: 0.69, 0.545, 1.267 and 1.052 from 0% to 50%+ short (q355). Most of the 2016 excess is timing, as F8 says. A small real effect in 2016 cannot be ruled out.

alternatives.explanation: The 'fade' could be the lapse itself rather than a warning sign before it. Comparing year t with t-1 measures stopping during year t. 'No Q4 order' is nearly part of the definition for a customer who stopped earlier in the year. The retained group's 1.0911 ratio also counts orders from customers new that year, who had no prior-year orders.
alternatives.test: (a) Kept only customers who also ordered in the prior year, and compared t-1 with t-2 (one year earlier), 2018-2024. (b) Tried a practical flag: first-half orders below half of the prior year's first half (prior first half of 4 or more orders). Counted how many lapsers it catches while they are still ordering in the second half.
alternatives.result: (a) Among existing customers, year-t orders over t-1 were 0.5986 for lapsers vs 1.0563 for retained (q359). One year earlier there is no fade: t-1 over t-2 was 1.086 for lapsers (n=1,758) vs 1.0493 for retained (n=16,538), with a median of 1.0 in both groups (q359). (b) Flagged customers lapsed at 0.1995 (n=1,644) against 0.0804 unflagged (q360). But flagged customers who still ordered after the first half lapsed at only 0.0495 (n=1,332, q360). Only 66 of 2,447 lapsers (0.027) were flagged while still reachable (q362). Lapsers' last orders were spread across quarters: 678 in Q1, 594 in Q2, 522 in Q3 and 653 in Q4 (q360).

alternatives.explanation: Lapse definition: some 'lapsers' come back, and the last year cannot be checked.
alternatives.test: Counted lapsers by year who ordered again in t+2 or later.
alternatives.result: Of each year's lapsers, 18-47 came back later. For example, 47 of the 300 in 2023 returned, while 2024's 272 can't be checked because 2025 is the last year (q358). This doesn't change the null, but 'lapse' includes one-year gaps. 458 of 465 2016 lapsers were onboarded before the records start (q358), so their history before 2016 is missing.

what_changed: 1) The evidence for 'short lines and returns don't predict lapse' is now a fixed-window, month-adjusted design (q354, q361). F8's annual-design ratios are dropped: they are subject to truncated exposure, and a month-adjusted version of the same design gives the opposite result (1.302-1.522, q349/q351). 2) 'Returns lower lapse' is dropped. Returns, including damaged or wrong-item returns, are simply not associated with lapse (q361). 3) The 2016 effect is mostly timing, but a modest residual (1.202, q356) remains possible. 4) The early-warning recommendation is withdrawn as stated. The fade happens in the final year, and there is none the year before (q359). A simple first-half-drop flag catches 66 of 2,447 lapsers while they are still ordering (q362). 5) The within-quarter comparison in q317 actually shows lapsers slightly higher in every quarter. Calling it 'close' is fair for Q1, Q2 and Q4, but Q3 is a visible gap; the fixed-window test (q354) is the better evidence.
revised_conclusion: Over 2017-2024, in a fixed-window test that adjusts each customer's short lines for their own branch and months, short lines don't predict whether a customer stops ordering for the next 12 months. The ratios were 0.98-1.078 across bands, with 4x+ at 1.028 (122 vs 118.7, n=3,269, q354). Returns, including damaged or wrong-item returns, show no link either (1.111, 36 vs 32.4, n=1,665, q361). The large 2016 excess for high-short customers mostly reflects when lapsing customers ordered. In a fixed window, a modest 1.202 remains (64 vs 53.3, q356), which could be a small real effect of the start-up stock-out or noise. Lapse is abrupt rather than gradual: lapsers' orders don't decline in the year before their final year (1.086 vs 1.0493, q359). Order-frequency drops mainly show customers who have already stopped, so they are not yet a useful early warning (66 of 2,447 lapsers flagged while reachable, q362). The evidence doesn't support funding a service-recovery programme on this link, and it doesn't support an order-fade watch list as an early warning either.
not_evidence_of: That service doesn't matter. Short lines might cut what customers buy (lost share of wallet) without ending the account; that wasn't tested here. Backorders filled later, delivery speed and service-contact quality weren't measured. The 2016 residual is not evidence that the stock-out drove customers away, and it doesn't clear it either. 'Lapse' is not confirmed churn: some lapsers return, 2024 is censored, and accounts may continue under another account id. The near-uniform return reason codes are a data-quality concern, not evidence about why goods came back.
